titleStmt.title: Interview with Gordon E. Gullikson, n.d.
titleStmt.author: Robert Babcock and Katherine Schilling [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Gordon E. Gullikson was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: -- Gullikson. He resides at 1100 Oak Avenue North, Onalaska, Wisconsin. His place of birth was Onalaska, Wisconsin. He was born 3/30 of 1918, and he's a white man. He was in the infantry in the wartime activity. He's a 1st Battalion, 22nd Infantry. From 1944 to 1945, he was a first lieutenant, Korea, and he was a captain in Korea with the 24th Infantry. He enlisted in 1943 to 1946, and also again from 1951 to 1953. A little double dipper.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did they call you back or did they --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: They called me.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Called you back.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: You know, the reason they called back -- the reason it was all small flight units. You couldn't use your tank. You couldn't use much of your artillery. You couldn't use your ammo. They went back and they got P38s and used them because those jets were too damn fast. You know, you couldn't -- straight like an airline with a jet. One squirt and he was gone.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Then they get these old P38s and, you know, 120 miles an hour. Boy, they could go up and down.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Go up and down. They work them bills.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: They worked those units.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Gordon, do you remember what you were doing on December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. I was going to go to a movie with my wife in Beloit, Wisconsin, and this is the first fight that I ever had with my wife at that time. I wanted to enlist the next day and she says no.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Said no way.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: But she was right, you know. Because we hadn't been married very long, and I was in on a new job and -- so it worked out fine. But later on I had a friend there in Blight and he was talking about this voluntary officer candidate school. I went to Rockford and took a test. It was eight lawyers and two farmers and a bartender and myself. Seven of the eight lawyers failed. It was a speed test. One hundred questions, 60 minute. And you know lawyers, he'd tried to figure out why it was right and why it was wrong. So you just go through and you get all the ones you knew absolutely, and then you could go back and -- so the farmers, the bartender, and myself, we aced it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Imagine that, huh?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: But then if you had a, you know, a good grade in basic training, because the last two weeks of your basics and they had you do kind of a corporal's job. You know, giving commands and stuff. Boy, that was fun.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So where did you take basic training?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Camp Lauderdale, Texas. I remember a while it was Texas.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And that was 1941 or '44?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Forty-four.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Forty-four.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. It was when I got my -- the hell did the war start?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Well, it started in '41, didn't it? December 7th.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. Must have been '42.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Forty-two.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. I remember that.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Because you were away for a while?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: But once you got in, when did you -- you went through basics, then you went to officer camp training?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Go and become an officer? And then what?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Then I went to Camp Lauderdale, Texas, and we were training recruits. I really liked that because, first of all, we got a lot of Mexican kids over there. And they would be the scraggliest-looking recruits that you ever saw. First of all, they had a lot of black hair. They loved black hair. The old barber cut through it easy. Christ, I thought they were going to kill that guy. Shit. They looked like a plucked chicken. But, you know, then 13 weeks later, you still see those on the drills going. Boy, they looked like young men. Before, they looked like hoodlums, you know. I really enjoyed that. But then -- well, we kind of acted -- you know, in this company sometimes we'd have as many as 20 second lieutenants, but they'd be there for two, three days. They would just kind of waiting for shipping dates. But I enjoyed that. But then I went to the Woodchoppers division. And we went on some maneuvers up in Washington, which was good.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Now, Woodchopper division. Tell me a little bit more about that.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: I wasn't with them very long, and they had multiple officers there to -- and once you showed a little promise, then you went to Providence, Rhode Island, and hopped a boat.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Hopped a boat? That's where the ship-off point was?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Providence, Rhode Island? What'd that feel like, when you got on that ship and head over, overseas? Did you have orders in hand as to where you were going?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. We were -- we were replacement officers for 4th Division. Took 21 of us. So we, you know, we swapped the breeze, you know. "Well, what's this? What do you think about it?" None of us knew a damn thing about it. And we got in to -- we went -- we landed at Liverpool, got on a train and went right to Dover and got on a ship, went right over. We landed in Utah Beach, but it was after the -- they had taken it, you know. So we just came in as replacements.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You were replacements for the guys after D-Day?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: But you still went on to Utah Beach?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. It was all a wreckage.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Must have been.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And the fortifications that Germany made. God, damn it. They had concrete teeth, you know, sticking out of the damn -- you couldn't see them in high tide. But, boy, at low tide, you know, they were just waiting to grab any boat that came along. And up on the hill there, directly ahead stuff. You know. Six-foot-wide, or -deep, concrete walls and stuff. The bombs and shelled and heard it much at all.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How did you take those? Just --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Flamethrower.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Just flamethrower?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. But it was tough getting the guy up there to do that.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: They were firing down; right?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. But I wasn't in on that part of the combat.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Right. But they came in and -- but you -- so then when you got onboard came in on Utah -- so you replaced an officer that had been hurt or --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Killed.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Killed on the beach or --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: -- taking the beach?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Up to that time I joined them at the (inaudible). And, you know, before that, they had causalities but there wasn't nothing great. But they went along pretty good. But they had a lot of trouble with these hedgerows. They're gnarly shrubs that have grown over the years and the farmers used them for fences. But, hell, you couldn't even saw them with a hacksaw, hardly.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: It's the water-wood type of stuff.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. And they would come in along there with their machine gun and you crash. Of course, you put in a tank, and the tank would go belly up, you know. Then they'd get them there with a shell, you know, in the soft part of the belly. It was --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Blow up part of the --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: They'd just shoot them then.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And, you know, that was new to American troops. It was a trial and error deal in a lot of this stuff. And then, you know -- thank goodness, you know, there was a sergeant there. He came up with the idea to put some metal prongs on the front of those tanks, which they welded them on, and the tank would burrow down into the hedgerow and then toss it up. Saved a lot of lives. Just a common sense, you know -- no general thought of it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: It was a sergeant?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: It was a sergeant that -- and that was true, you know. In the field, you do with what you got. Not what your supposed to have. And it was -- a lot of people that came up some damn good ideas. And that wasn't too hard to get them to try because, you know, these fields generals, you know, they want to look good. Boy, they have an ego that's (lifts thumb.) And I think in a lot of cases, they really don't -- they say they care about all the men but they just keep throwing you into a hopeless situation and so that they would look good. I hate to say that but I think that's true.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you commanded a company, or --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: No. I was a machine gun platoon leader --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: -- when I joined.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And that was a 60 caliber or what kind of machine gun?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, it was a 30 caliber. It was water-cooled. And then we had the regular barrels and stuff. But you burn those barrels out pretty fast. These guys, they get to a machine, they'll run through a belt of ammunition in a hurry. You know. The waste was just terrible. But it was good morale, you know. When a guy's firing a gun, he feels like he's in charge. And when he runs out of ammunition, then he feels helpless.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: I've been there. Well, I told people that when somebody's firing at you, you cannot believe how flat you want to get to that ground.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's just how it was. If you could flatten out like a pancake, you would. Well, so -- when you went in and took over, let's -- how long was it from then to that Hürtgen Forest?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Sixteen days.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Sixteen days later? And then tell me more about how that came to be. When you came up to that.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, we would -- in the platoon, leaders, you know, the rifle companies, they would attack and we would all try to line up to with machine guns to give support to the attacker. Well, it wasn't always possible because you're field of vision was limited, but -- well, one A Company was supposed to come down this side and, and I had six machine guns. And I was supposed to tie on to A Company when they went on into the attack. Well, they never showed up. And we were in a -- we were depilated. And those Germans knew where we were in because they were prepared for that, top of that hill. We were safe under that hill, but they were really pumping lead at us. So I took that, my runner and I, we went out around to first of all to see where those machine gunners were. And to see where A Company was. But they had -- well, they'd gotten hung up, you know, a couple hundred yards back. But we got down there and kind of looked down on a little spot there and somebody was, had a little fire in a 55-gallon drum. You know, four or five guys huddled around it, you know. But at the time our runner, Rocky, and I realized that they were Germans. And they realized that we were Americans. And it didn't take long, boy, to haul ass. And we went through, there was some willows along there about that big. And we went through there just like they were like wheat, you know. When I got to the hospital -- Christ, I was beat to death. No shit. But I got out around. We got out around a little depilated spot and I said, "Rocky." I said, "Boy, we were really lucky there." And then we knew where we could go back and unload on those Germans with our mortars. And just about that time a mortar dropped right behind in him. From here to that TV. Just one big blast, you know. And it knocked me down and I knew that I was hit but I didn't know where. Of course, I had a lot of god damn clothes on and you couldn't see any blood or anything. Well, it hit me right in the shoulder socket. Came right in here. Just missed my heart. And that went in into my shoulder socket. And -- then there was some blood there and I said, "Rocky." I kind of felt like I was losing it. I said, "Slap me! Slap me across the face." "No, I can't do that." And I said, "Just slap me." Because I was afraid I was going to faint. So he did. He felt so bad. But we, he took me out and I kind of leaned on him and we went back to where the aid station was. Then I saw that place. And then they flew me to England. Well, they wouldn't take the-- I still got the shrapnel in my shoulder. They wouldn't take it out because you'd lose your fluid there. And then you'd lose the use of your arm. So I still tickle the old machines when I go on an airplane.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: I bet. Still got a piece of shrapnel.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And that was what? The day of the Hürtgen Forest or day two of the --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Oh, no. That was about the -- oh, let's see. Well, they'd been battling at the Hürtgen Forest before we got there. And, shit, they'd gain 20 yards one day and they'd lose it the next. It was really a sad situation. And I wasn't there long enough to really get the full gist of it. Voice: Excuse me. Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah? So some of those guys, you know, had been there for 30 days going through there. They were trying to go through. Because they had two divisions try to go through before and we went in and relieved them because they were depleted. And when we left the Hürtgen Forest, I don't think we were 25 percent strength.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: They just chewed us up, huh?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: You'd have two, three men to a squad, you know.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Well, I saw in Band of Brothers, they had one of the episodes was on the Hürtgen Forest. They just tore up even that group.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So -- so you got the Purple Heart over there in --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Bronze Star. Bronze Star?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. And I got -- well, I was promoted to first lieutenant and when I got to Korea, I relieved the company commander there and I was made captain.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Tell me about Korea a little bit. What --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, I was a very ambitious young man. I loved the shoe business, and I was working, I thought, for a damn good company. For all Jews, you know. And they say, "How in the hell did a Norwegian ever get into this damn place?" And I'm telling you, every barrel of pickle needs a little dill in it to spice them up you know. And, oh, they razzed the shit out of me. But you know with the Jews. First of all, if they razz you, you know they like you. They don't tell me the damndest thing. But I produced, and that's all you got to do with the Jews. Do a good job and produce. And then --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You were in the shoe business?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, I was a -- I was a supervisor. I was a manager and then a district manager and then a regional manager. You get a bigger territory to take care of.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Was that for the suit company?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: We sold shoes from everybody. Wherever we could buy shoes that fit our little -- you know, we had popular priced shoes. We had everything from house slippers to nylon hose.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. So when you -- so you got out of the army in 1946?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And then you --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And my little girl was six years old at that time. So we started -- we wanted to have another child. So I went to the doctor and he said, "You have a good case of malaria." So I was sterile for 11 years. It was 11 years between my two girls. But every once in a while this malaria would flare up. I was taking inventory one time. Freeport, Illinois. And you just, you just sweat profusely. And you just sweat all over. And needed -- hell, I just rolled up on the rug on the floor there, trying to keep warm. And you’re sweating like hell and you can't get warm.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: I don't know how I drove home to Beloit from Freeport. Hell, it's about 35 miles. You think you just get into bed and you just -- you're there for two, three, four days. And the perspiration is just yellow. Looks like you pissed the bed, you know. And that week is an attack. But --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Then you come back and you're all right?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So when you commanded the 24th Infantry in Korea, Korea's a totally different war, then.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, not entirely different. You've lost all of your might and power that we felt that we had, because those people, they would have a nylon sack of rice around their neck. That was their rations for ten days. That's how they supplied it. And they didn't all have rifles. They'd go and they’d attack, and one guy falls down, and if he had a rifle, the other guy'd come along and pick it up and then he'd have a rifle.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And they were tough, you know. They're small in stature. We had some that -- when we were making fortifications, and -- you know, you never loaf in the army. They always find something for you to do. But, anyhow, we were going to put up this big concrete, barbed wire thing, and we had some Koreans that were, you know, North Koreans -- or South Koreans. And they would work for us just for food, you know. And we'd get two GIs. You put a pole in between two rolls of barbed wire. The rolls of barbed wire were 80 pounds a piece. And you’d have -- it'd be 160 pounds. Two GIs, great, big, strapping guys going up the hill with it. A little Korean, he had a little wood situated on the back. He’d put two on his back and he'd go up. And he weighed about 130 pounds.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Wow. That really opened your eyes about the --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And, you know, they never sat down; they'd all sit on their haunches. Ten minute break. Sit right down on their haunches. They never sat on the ground.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: The North Koreans were a tough group.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yes, they were.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: They still are.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, it's the same kind of stuff that you guys fought. We are just not equipped. We're clodhoppers instead of ballet dancers, you know?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Well, that's true. Not so different now.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. Because, you know, first of all, if you kill one, it doesn't make any difference. They just keep coming. They don't cry and mull over their losses. And, by God, they're tough. And, you know, they’ll come around from the damndest -- over these mountains and they will hold the places you wouldn't think humans would be. They're there. And what they would do, too -- of course, MacArthur, you know, he had a -- oh, boy. And they drove us all the way down to Pusan. Why, with just a little -- they just about drove us into the ocean. And then they got troops from Japan and then they stabilized that, but --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So they were trying to push you back into the ocean?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They just about had us too.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How did that -- were they just attacking and you guys would fall back?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, yeah. They'd go through -- first of all, we had -- when you put troops on a basic line over a period of time, they deteriorate. They're not worth a shit. They're too lazy. You got to keep people in the army working. Doesn't matter what. Just digging a goddamn hole. Keep them digging. And, oh, god, they went through us like ___+. Of course, it's all Koreans were there. We’d put a division on the line and put American divisions right behind them so they wouldn't run through. You know, it’s their country. Jesus Christ. They're not fighters; I think they were lovers. But, boy, these North Koreans, I'm worried about that because -- first of all, out here, he’s said he’s got a million-man army. And that little damn country. They're poor as hell and, you know, the kids are starving and, boy, they put on a parade you just wouldn't believe. I don't know if you've seen them goosestepping there once in a while but --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: I don't know want to mess with the North Koreans, no.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And it seems like they'll, you know -- well. I think they’re typical Asians. Life is not that important to them. Not like you and I. And, you know, somebody dies. "Well, that’s too bad. Move them over. Somebody else take his place."

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Now, you fought -- it says here you fought in Germany too. So once you --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: France, Germany, and then Korea.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you went in on Utah Beach. Hürtgen Forest was France?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: No. Germany.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That was Germany?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And then after the Hürtgen Forest -- well, you were wounded?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So did you go back to the --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So after you're wounded, you went back out and then you were back as a platoon leader again?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Then you went on into Germany at that point?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. We wound up almost to the Austrian border when the war was over. But the fighting -- well, it was bad in some places but, you know, you take some causalities but you take your objective, you know. But it’s really demoralizing to attack, attack, attack, take losses and don't take your objective.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yeah. Well, I mean you got to be able to say "Yeah, I did it." Isn't that the truth? Well, take us back to that time, Gordon. What -- I mean, you guys literally saved America and you saved the world from some unpleasant things.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: That's true.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: When you guys came back as a group and you formed, like, this association -- how long have you been active in the association?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Since day one.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Since day one?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: First of all, Chaplin Boise is a good friend of mine. And he was the one that started it. And, first of all, in the shoe business, you have samples that you make. And they always make a sample. That's the best -- that's what you show to the public. And they always took men’s shoes, size seven, which is real small. And that's what Chaplin Boise wore. So I furnished him with some of the finest shows he's ever had. Because preachers, you know, are not too well off to start with. And he really appreciated it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Always had good shoes.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Oh, god, he had good shoes. Well, I called him before I came down here. But I found him down ___+. And he's just a -- he's a saint. And he's so honest and so fair and so smart. And he's a talented guy. God, he can play organs, he can play -- he's a wonderful preacher, God.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: When you started these meetings, was it kind of like Bob said? You’d have a hotel room, a little conference room, and get together with the wives and --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And most of the things were -- well, they'd be just, like -- well, it wouldn't be anything this big, you know, but we'd have church. A lot of our meals would be in the church. And it didn't cost much to go.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: No, it didn't.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And, you know, he had a lot of talented people in his church. And, you know, we'd go little places around. Plenty of places to go. So it wasn't expensive. And, you know, he had a core group with a good group. But it was mostly officers. Some of them, you know, they're -- they're still some of here.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Still formal?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, god. You -- and, you know, you kind of taste like sour. First of all, I was a good officer. I’m not blowing smoke up my ass. I tried to do everything I could to take the objective with the least amount of causalities. We had to take a bridge line up there, and you could see them taking in the bridge line. And we were sitting down there. We had to take those suckers the next day. And there was four 50-caliber machine guns guarding the bridge from the Air Corps. They'd been sitting there for three weeks and never fired a round, you know. Because North Korea didn't have any Air Force. I was going to get my ass kicked out of the Army because I said, "Shit. You guys been setting here," I said, "forever. You got to blow the smoke out of those barrels there once in a while or something." I said, "So how about giving up a little support fire." "Yeah, yeah, yeah." They were ready to go.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: They were ready to go. They were bored up there.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: So when we took off running, boy, they just -- and those Quad 50s, you know, they really chew up rocks in a hurry. And they just went up and down that coastline. You see those Koreans haul ass over their point. We took that hill. We only had one causality, one wounded. But I never even told anybody about it because I was sure they'd kick my ass out of the Army, which wouldn't have been all bad either.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Wouldn't have been all that bad.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: But, you know, it just sucked like that, you know. And other places you put on a patrol base, you know. Put on, say, one company heavily armed. Well, you know, maybe a mile or two in front of the main line. Well, every once in a while, you know they'd be firing back and forth and sputtering and stuff but nothing -- but every once in a while they'd have three, four companies behind here and they'd just snuff out a patrol base. And this one colonel says, "Now, what we got to do. We got to build a concrete fence on both sides all the way back to our --" What do you call it? I says, "You, you want this platoon patrol to come all the way back in a goddamn chute like that?" He said they couldn't come in, and I said, "You got to have them so they can maneuver. They got to go this way, they got to go that way, whichever way they’re coming to move." You know. He never made the building, but I was just scared as shit he was going to do it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Make you a little chute.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: For Christ’s sake. I mean, Thompson said -- maybe the book said something about it. It had pretty pictures in there but -- shit. And then they’d rotate the battalion commanders. I always felt maybe -- I was not prejudice against color but all’s well, we got the shit end of the stick, as far as the division was concerned. You know, if you had an Italian commander someplace that fucked up, they'd send him to us, you know. That was just punishment.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: He had to come to the 22nd --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. But then I got an Italian commander. He’d been in the service for 25 years at Fort Benning as Motor Officer. And he was the nicest guy. And he could tell you every nut, screw, and bolt in a car. But he didn't know which end the shell came out of the rifle. God almighty. And the nicest guy. It was cold, you know. "You got to put your flappers down." I said, "When you walk in a line, you don’t put your flappers down. You can hear artillery coming, and if you put your flappers down, you can't hear." "Oh, no. Regulation." We went down there. Shit, a shell dropped up there about 75 yards. "Oops. I'll put the --"

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's the end of that.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Didn't hear anymore about that.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Well, do you think -- is there -- I think we've pretty much went over where you were and what you did and all. Do you have any recollections for future people that might be interested to learn about something you'd like to add?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well -- and a lot of this is hearsay. You know, I don't have -- but in Korea, officers were a dime a dozen because you had to lead. You couldn't push them. Especially the Blacks. They’d fight good if you were behind them and you were pushing and you do this, "I'll be there." But if you sat back in headquarters and tell them where to go, shit, they'd never get there. So I, I was -- lost my train of thought now.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Had to lead them?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. It'll come back.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Well, you were talking about the thought you’d like to leave with somebody about that time.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Oh, oh, yeah. The casualty rate for second lieutenants was very high in Korea because it was all small units firing. And, you know, you didn't have the tanks with you. You didn't have the firepower that we always depend on. And -- oh. Well, they got a lot of West Point officers over there. You know, they ground them up pretty fast. So that's when they, they needed first sergeant and staff sergeant and first and second lieutenants. You know, squad leaders, really. So that is what -- but when you got that group that were recalled in Spokane, Washington. They were the biggest drunks. They were not going to go back. One guy had ten spots on his body. He got ten Purple Hearts in World War II. "You think I’m going back? Throw me in jail. I don't give a shit." You know, a lot of them -- first of all, they had that attitude. And, you know, I was pissed off. Jesus, I had to -- you know, I had a career to go and I had, you know, wife and child. I was just building a house. You know, it just wasn't fair.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So they just recalled you? They sent a letter and said, "we need you"?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Report to (?)POOE(?) in Seattle. And then people -- I was always asked -- 24th, 22nd infantry. "Oh, god. Gordon. I'm sure glad I’m not going." I didn't know what the 22nd infantry was. I didn’t know they were all Black.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Oh, the 24th infantry was Black?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. Anyhow, we get to Seattle, and we had a little so-called refresher course or something. When I went down to Fort Sherida, when I had to sign up down there, it was kind of sleeting and raining. The old sergeant says, "You ever fire a .45?" And I said, "Yeah. I never hit much with it, but --" He says, "Come with me." So I got out and I fired five rounds into Lake Michigan. And "You qualified," he goes. That was it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's good enough. You're good.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Shit, man. I had five dead ones after I got through it. That's the sorriest piece of material I've ever seen. Boy, those crops, they had those Lukers. God, they were a nice pistol. It was the prize, boy, to get a hold of one of those --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So -- okay. Can you think of anything else? Or --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Well, I don't know how they would solve the problem of not using up their West Point. But, you know, that's -- that's the backbone of the service in the years to come.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Right. Oh, that's right.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: One of these great -- whether they were getting ___+ or not, but they’d probably make a pretty good soldier.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Man, they're --

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: You know, it just feels that you kind of got screwed, you know, and some of these guys -- well, I know -- some friend of mine. I think they joined and a year in 1940. At just one year enlisted --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: One year?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah, it stretched out to six.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Bet they were really pissed off.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Oh, shit. They got over to the Far East, they couldn't find him.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: I bet not.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Oh, my brother. My brother was in the Marines. First of all, he wanted to be - he’s a big, husky guy. He wanted to get in the Air Force. Well, he failed. He was too big. But -- and he was pissed off. So he goes off and joins the Marines. Well, it was back and forth. I said, " Christ, all mighty." I said, "You guys," I said, "you know, you get awards, you know, for having a good bowl movement, for Christ’s sake, in the Marines, you know." Sharpshooter First Class. Sharpshooter Second Class. Christ, he’d have those damn things. "Shit," I said. "We’ll go to PX and get Cracker Jack boxes. You don’t have to do that." So we had a good rapport, but he had one of these -- oh, it's a -- it's a machine where you can -- landing machine. You take troops in and take the wounded and the dead back to the ship. Ship them to the shore back. And he says, "Boy, those Marines really took a whacking on some of those islands." And, you know, "The admiral said, well, they’re going to go to this island, Peleliu. Take them three days." They were there 71 days and had 27,000 causalities. Then they never used the goddamn thing. They were going to use it for an air strike.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: 27,000 causalities? Jesus.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: You know, but you -- you suppose those guys would ever admit they made a mistake --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: -- and pull back? Well, hell, those Japs were there and they'd been there for years, you know, and they dug down. And that bamboo was just like steel. When you had bunkers made of bamboo, boy, they were good. Because they were workmen. You know, they worked those things -- and you just couldn’t lodge along them. Christ, you had those ships out there hurling, you know, 500-pound shells out there. They’d be there when the smoke cleared.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Oh. And in Korea, well, of course, MacArthur -- you know, he was a big showoff. Wading along from a little landing, but he got water on his shoes and dug out. Dug. He had -- he was a smart -- but he would get, geared up some tanks and, boy, they'd go up, you know, this valley. Shit, the Koreans would come around and blow the opening shut. Shot them up piecemeal. They couldn't get out. And then after that you had the ridges on both sides. And that was tough.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That was dug in?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. And, you know, then Ridgway came along. And he was, he was a general. He was -- and I got that -- you know that -- I was the most experienced line officer in the battalion. And they wanted to make me S3. So I went up there for a while and at one time, there was this one general. He was a strapping guy. Boy, did he ride these battalion commanders over. Well, he called them everything but a white man, you know. "So-and-so’s wounded." "Where was he wounded?" "I don't know." "Damn it. It’s your job, boy. You go to --" Oh, boy, he would really rip them out. That's my first experience. God, I’d have been scared to talk to him. No. They offered me if I stayed, you know. But, you know, and I'm not even going to join the Methodist church now.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Wouldn’t join that.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: I wasn’t joining shit. But it's been a great life and a great career. I just -- I'm so proud you, know? All four of them. Four brothers. Three brothers. All four of us are in the service. You know, there aren’t too many, four out of one family.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: No. I think my dad and my uncle went out of his family of seven. Growing up, I think he had two brothers.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: And when -- you know, your dad and your uncle, they didn't want to talk about it because, you know, you’ve got five guys that feel bad or feel like draft dodgers or whatever. And so, you know, if they talk about it, well, all it does is make them feel bad. So that's maybe a lot of the reason why they don't really talk about it to the family. Of course, a lot of men aren’t much on conversation, anyhow. Especially the old-timers.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: No. True, true. Well, Gordon, I think we're there.

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: Yeah. Well --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So is there anything else you want to say in conclusion?

sp.speaker: Gordon E. Gullikson
sp.p: I was pleased to do this interview and I would like to help hone it up to make it fit -- give it, sent it to somebody else.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right.
